WASHINGTON: US P resident Donald Trump said on Wednesday (Nov 4) the Iran war has been worth it despite acknowledging its role in losses in US midterm elections in which his Republican party lost control of Congress. "The Iran thing we had to do, and we continue to do it," he told reporters. T he Iran war was responsible for a spike in gasoline prices that were seen as a strong factor in why Democrats made big gains in the elections. T rump said the war has been worth it to stop Tehran from "having a nuclear weapon."

"I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different," Trump said. Trump also again said that if he had been on the ballot, he believed "we would have won." "But they just, you couldn't transfer that love. There was such love at those rallies, it was incredible and we weren't able to transfer the love to candidates," he said.

JERUSALEM: Benjamin Netanyahu 's political rivals seize d on Democrats' capture of the US Congress as proof that he had squandered generations of bipartisan American support for Israel, as they seek a chance to form a government without him. Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and Ho us e in Tuesday's (Nov 3) midterm election, in a scathing rebuke to US President Donald Trump fuelled in part by deep fr us tration over the unpopular US -Israeli war on Iran. The US vote took place j us t a week after an Israeli election, when Netanyahu 's right-wing coalition lost its parliamentary majority but performed well enough to deny his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot a clear path to unseat him. Israeli President Isaac Herzog is due to hold talks on Wednesday and Thursday with party representatives before tasking one of the two men with forming the next government. Meanwhile Netanyahu remains prime minister as a caretaker.

US SUPPORT WAVERS FOR LONGSTANDING ALLY The United States has been Israel's staunchest ally for generations under presidents of both parties, providing billions of dollars a year in military aid since the 1970s. But unlike previo us leaders who assiduo us ly courted Democrats and Republicans alike, Netanyahu has openly backed Republicans. Support for Israel among Democrats and some Republicans wavered after Israel launched its military assault in Gaza following the 2023 Hamas attack, and fell further t his year since Trump and Netanyahu ordered a joint attack on Iran. Some Democratic candidates made criticism of American military aid to Israel a prominent campaign argument. On Tuesday, Trump, who had endorsed Netanyahu , made an election-day pledge to halt US$4 billion in annual funding to Israel, a move he said would take away a "bad talking point" us ed by Democrats. Yair Golan, head of Israel's centre-left opposition Democrats party, said on X that the US midterm election results "reveal j us t how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans". Centrist opposition leader Yair Lapid said the results showed "Israel cannot afford" for Netanyahu to remain in office. "It endangers our security, it jeopardises our democracy, and it will ruin our standing on the global stage," Lapid said in a social media post.

Netanyahu has so far remained silent about the outcome of the US vote. His office did not respond to a request for comment. It could be weeks or months before it becomes clear whether it is Netanyahu or Eisenkot who ultimately faces the task of repairing the relationship. Whichever candidate is chosen first m us t build a new coalition or the other will be given an opportunity. If both fail, a new election would be called. Meanwhile, Udi Sommer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University, predicted that the incoming Democratic-controlled US Congress would be the most adversarial towards Israel in its his tory. Although most power over foreign policy still resides with the president, Democrats could apply pressure through hearings, congress ional oversight and budgetary measures, he said. "The Democratic landslide and the Republican wipeout encapsulate the next chapter in US -Israel relations," Sommer said.

IRAN: Iran's government savoured the stinging rebuke delivered to Donald Trump in the midterm elections, declaring voters had rejected the war launched by the US president even as Tehran remained on high alert for the possibility of renewed strikes. "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran's chief negotiator, posted on X on Wednesday (Nov 4), adding that Washington should not ignore public opinion by attacking his country again. Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said in a written statement that US hostility would persist regardless of which party was in power, warning against "even the slightest inclination towards submission" to the US . "The US sees the end of its hegemony as distant; we see it as near," he added. OLD FOES

Democrats captured majorities in both the Senate and Ho us e in Tuesday's election , with victories in Republican strongholds underscoring deep fr us tration with Trump 's stewardship of the economy and his decision to launch a war that drove up gas prices. In Iran, a news outlet run by the judiciary shared a joke circulating on X that " Trump failed at regime change in Iran but he succeeded in Texas", a reference to the southern state where a Democrat won a Senate race for the first time in decades. But two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that while Iranian leaders welcomed the Democrats’ victory, Tehran was concerned that Trump could seek to compensate for it with a military strike, and remained on high alert. Iran's leaders have long regarded the United States as their main enemy, referring to it as "the Great Satan". At a state-organised rally on Wednesday commemorating the student takeover of the US embassy in Tehran during the 1979 Islamic revolution, demonstrators voiced triumph at an election they linked to Iran's success in surviving months of US attacks. "The fact that the might of these warmongering Republicans has been broken, something unprecedented in human history, means that from now on we will see the real war unfolding inside the US Senate and among American officials ," said one, giving only his family name of Nazari.

Pictures of US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, on a dartboard during the 47th anniversary of the US expulsion from Iran, in Tehran, Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: West Asia News Agency via REUTERS/Majid Asgaripour)

Mediators have intensified efforts to end the war amid fears it could reignite after the election , with Trump on Tuesday declining to rule out a resumption of combat operations after the vote and Iran planning wider retaliation if war resumes. The US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28, and Iran responded with strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. Conflict also erupted in Lebanon between Iran-backed Hezbollah and Israel, and more recently spread to Yemen, from where the Iran-aligned Houthis have struck energy facilities, airports and other targets in Saudi Arabia. Global oil and gas prices have shot up with shipping through the Strait of Hormuz severely disrupted after Tehran declared it closed, while the US has imposed a naval blockade on Iran, hitting Iran's economy hard. "IRAN'S SHADOW OVER US ELECTIONS" Ahead of the US election, senior Iranian officials told Reuters that Tehran was deliberately prolonging talks with the US to weaken Trump politically ahead of the vote. Some news outlets played on the timing of the election on the anniversary of the embassy seizure, when radical students cemented Iran's toppling of the US -backed Shah by storming the embassy and holding 52 Americans hostage there for 444 days. Major Iranian newspaper Hamshahri linked the events with a front-page image showing Trump blindfolded with his head bowed. With a headline declaring "Iran's shadow over US elections", it said Washington had been "47 years Iran's captive: from the capture of the spies' nest ( US embassy) to the November 2026 US Congress elections". The Iran war has been unpopular among Americans since it began, and blaming the war for driving up costs was a foc us of the Democrats' election campaign. Khamenei's message signalled that Tehran had no intention of showing flexibility on its demands for lasting control over the Strait of Hormuz or conditions to end the conflict. "The consequences of ( US ) miscalculations and arrogant del us ions have manifested as a heavy burden of costs, borne by the American people and the puppet regimes subservient to the US government," he said. Trump has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war that is now in its ninth month. "I think a part of it was Iran, but at the same time people understood the importance of what I've done with Iran," Trump told Fox News, referring to the election result. The conservative Iranian newspaper Jam-e Jam declared the election result "The twilight of Trump ism".

Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms' win marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground.

WASHINGTON: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms won Georgia’s race for governor on Tuesday (Nov 3), becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US state and delivering Democrats a victory in one of the nation's most closely divided political battlegrounds. The former Atlanta mayor, who will also be the first female governor of the state, defeated Republican businessman Rick Jackson, according to US media projections. She succeeds Republican Governor Brian Kemp, who is leaving office after serving two consecutive terms. Bottoms, 56, also previously served as a senior adviser to former President Joe Biden and director of the White House Office of Public Engagement.

Former US President Barack Obama speaks as Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Democratic gubernatorial nominee Keisha Lance Bottoms listen during a rally ahead of the midterm elections in Morrow, Georgia, US on Oct 28, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Edgar Su)

The victory marked a new milestone for Black women in American politics, who have long been a core base within the Democratic Party but remain underrepresented in the nation’s highest elected offices. The same evening, Stacey Plaskett was elected governor of the US Virgin Islands, a US territory, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of a US jurisdiction.

Bottoms' win also marks a significant shift in Georgia state politics, where Black voters have formed a central part of the Democratic coalition that helped to turn the reliably Republican state into a national battleground. Republicans had controlled the governor’s office for more than two decades. Jackson, the billionaire founder of healthcare staffing company Jackson Healthcare, cast himself as a political outsider and campaigned on tax cuts, public safety and reducing government regulation. Bottoms’ victory comes eight years after fellow Democrat Stacey Abrams became the first Black woman nominated for governor by a major US political party. Abrams lost governor's races in Georgia in 2018 and 2022, but her campaigns helped to build a multigenerational, multiracial coalition that boosted Democratic turnout, helped elect two Democratic US senators and delivered Georgia’s electoral votes to a Democratic presidential candidate for the first time in decades.

COPENHAGEN: Greenland's parliament on Tuesday (Nov 3) ratified the Arctic island's security agreement struck earlier this year with US President Donald Trump, although some opposition party members questioned the deal's economic value. The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September, aimed at ending tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the strategically located and mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory. The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, paving the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination. A majority of lawmakers had already signalled support for the deal in a first debate last month.

Tuesday's vote was 16 in favour and none against, with seven abstentions. The White House in January said Trump was discussing options for acquiring Greenland, including potential use of the US military, alarming governments in Europe and triggering intense diplomatic efforts to calm the situation. Greenlandic Foreign Minister Mute Egede said on Tuesday that ratification of the deal was an important step for the island. "We must accept that peace and stability are no longer something we can take for granted," Egede told lawmakers in Nuuk shortly before the vote. Opposition party Naleraq, the most prominent political voice for Greenland's independence, questioned the deal's economic value during the debate. "We are looking for a better agreement that we can benefit from when we become an independent state. But no economic benefit has been gained from the agreement," Naleraq chair Pele Broberg said. The Danish parliament is due to give the bill a first reading on Nov 11, followed by a second reading and a vote on Nov 19. The executive agreement will enter into force once Denmark and Greenland have ratified it, and does not require approval from the US Senate.

Democrats, Trump face off after elections as Washington heads for divided government

Voters in conservative bastions who had propelled US President Donald Trump to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats.

WASHINGTON: Democrats and Republicans squared up on Wednesday (Nov 4) for what could be two years of deadlock in Washington, with the resurgent Democrats vowing to use their resounding midterm election victory to rein in US President Donald Trump, who signalled he was ready to continue flexing the executive branch's considerable powers. A wave of anger over Trump's policies , particularly the US-Iran war's role in pushing the cost of living higher, helped Democrats take the Senate, where they flipped seats in deeply Republican states for a majority of at least 54-44, and the House of Representatives, where they gained at least 25 seats. It will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress. "The American people have connected that corruption into the adverse impact of the policies that have taken place over the last two years," House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told MS NOW on Wednesday, promising to "make sure that wrongdoers are being held accountable."

Jeffries, a New York lawmaker who is on track to become the first Black speaker of the House, said Democrats would "work hard" on making life more affordable, while urging Trump to end his unpopular eight-month-old war against Iran before the next Congress is seated. Trump, meanwhile, posted an image on social media of one of his signature red "Make America Great Again" baseball caps with the usual slogan replaced with the word "VETO", a reminder that Democrats will be limited in their ability to legislate without his support. Top Senate Republican John Thune, a veteran lawmaker not generally regarded as a firebrand, signaled that his caucus was not yet ready to look to a future beyond Trump. "Senate Republicans will not stand idly by as the far-left, socialist wing of the Democrat Party attempts to unwind everything we've done," Thune, of South Dakota, said in a statement. "Thankfully, we still have President Trump in the White House, and we'll work with him to stop the worst impulses of Democrat extremism."

US Senator Jon Ossoff (D-GA) waves to supporters during an election night rally after winning reelection in the US midterm elections, in Atlanta, Georgia on Nov 3, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Carlos Barria)

TEXAS, SOUTH CAROLINA, KANSAS FLIP Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to "pretend I'm on the ballot," a message that Democratic Party leaders were happy to amplify. The result: voters in conservative strongholds who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats , fuelled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high cost of living and anger at Trump's stewardship of the country. In Texas, the biggest Republican-led state before Tuesday, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate. Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remained uncalled as of Wednesday morning, leaving open the possibility that the Democrats ' majority could grow by another two seats to 56-44.

Related:

Trump says will accept results of US midterm election, NYT reports

Commentary: What to watch for in the US midterm elections

Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump's administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump's nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. However, until then, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead - a measure to fund the federal government past December - that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period. Trump, who is barred by the US Constitution from seeking a third term, has exercised an iron grip on his party for most of the last decade. He congratulated Democrats for doing "a good job," in uncharacteristically conciliatory media interviews overnight. He acknowledged the war with Iran had played a role in his party's losses but stood by his decision. He also said he would work with Democrats on issues such as immigration, though he threatened to veto any "insane" bills they passed. Vice President JD Vance, who may run as a possible Trump successor in the 2028 presidential election, piled all the blame on his boss's decision to join Israel to attack Iran in February. "The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote in a long social media post. "The president himself said so last night. If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay."

Supporters celebrate outside the venue for the election night rally of Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed during the US midterm elections in Detroit, Michigan, US, on Nov 4, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Dieu-Nalio Chery)

DEMOCRATIC WAVE Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump's expensive tariffs on imports, some of which were ruled to be an illegal tax by the courts, and the war with Iran for driving up costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House. Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats for defending transgender people's rights and similar social issues, portraying them as radical and extreme. But voters made it clear they were far more concerned with pocketbook issues. The Democratic wave flooded huge swaths of the country. Republicans lost ground in 99 per cent of the approximately 2,100 counties where most votes had been counted as of Wednesday morning , according to tallies compiled by Reuters and USA Today. Democrats made gains in the richest counties and the poorest; in counties where more people have college degrees and where fewer do. Democrats ' advances were particularly sharp in heavily Latino counties, including the border counties of Texas that shifted toward Trump in 2024 and the agricultural towns of the Kansas prairie.

Related:

Keisha Lance Bottoms wins Georgia race, becomes first Black woman elected governor of US state

Historic leadership firsts for minorities across US in midterm vote

Democrats flipped more than two dozen House seats currently held by Republicans, locking in a majority. Democrats won all the closely contested House races that have been decided so far, and they won about a dozen races in districts that Trump won by double digits two years ago. Abdul El-Sayed, a Democrat from the party's rising left wing, won Michigan's open Senate seat, becoming the first Muslim elected to the chamber. He defeated Mike Rogers, a former congressman and FBI agent, who entered the race with Trump's backing and sought to falsely portray El-Sayed, an Egyptian American born in Michigan, as a religious extremist. "You chose hate, and Michigan chose hope," El-Sayed told cheering supporters on Tuesday night, referring to Rogers. The night included several historic firsts for both parties. In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor of any US state; Byron Donalds won Florida's gubernatorial race to become the first Black Republican elected governor in the US and in New Mexico Deb Haaland became the country's first Native American woman to be elected governor. Democrat Gina Hinojosa will become the first Latina governor in Texas, while Democrat Xavier Becerra will be California's first Latino elected governor.
